passage: Tuesday. Sofia has been full of surprises. This morning I asked the baker if she had seeded bread, and she shook her head side to side and said "Da." I froze. In my head, a head shake meant no, but she seemed to be saying yes. She handed me the loaf, so it was yes. My classmate Sangeeta, who's lived here two years, laughed for a full minute. She told me that in Bulgaria the meanings of nodding and shaking are the reverse of what I'm used to. She also said back home some people nod to show they're listening, not that they agree. Lesson learned: when in doubt, use words. I'll say "yes" and "no" out loud, and show my palms. - Lakshmi

qa.q: What did Lakshmi ask the baker for?
qa.a: She asked if she had seeded bread.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling when the baker shook her head and said 'Da'?
qa.a: She was confused and frozen, because the head shake she knew as no came with a word that meant yes.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi decide to do in cross-cultural situations?
qa.a: She decided to use words, saying yes and no out loud, since gestures can mean different things.

qa.q: How might the baker have seen Lakshmi's reaction?
qa.a: She may have found it puzzling that a customer froze, since to her a head shake and 'Da' both meant yes.

grounding: A young adult learns that nodding and head shaking can mean different things, as in Bulgaria, and clarifies with words.

Omkar: the client's manager nodded the whole call. I think they agreed on the price!!
Tushar: did she say yes?
Omkar: no words, only nodding. I nodded back and said we'd send the contract
Tushar: hmm. in some places nodding just means "I'm following you", not "I agree"
Omkar: seriously??
Tushar: yes. and in a couple of countries a nod or shake means the opposite of what we're used to. ask in words

Tushar: yes, something like "Just to confirm, are you happy with the price?" 🙂
Omkar: on it. thank you 🙏

qa.q: How did the client's manager behave during the call?
qa.a: She nodded the whole call, with no words.

qa.q: How did Omkar feel on learning that a nod may not mean yes?
qa.a: Omkar felt alarmed, saying 'oh no', after assuming the manager agreed and promising a contract, then relieved to have a plan to email.

qa.q: What does Tushar advise Omkar to do?
qa.a: He advises asking in words, by emailing to confirm whether the manager is happy with the price.

qa.q: How might the client's manager see Omkar nodding back and promising a contract?
qa.a: She may think he has misunderstood, since she only meant that she was following.

grounding: A young adult learns nodding may show attention, not agreement, and that meanings vary across cultures, so words clarify.

passage:
For his agricultural extension training, Bhupen spent a week in a village near Sehore explaining a new drip-irrigation method to a group of farmers under a peepal tree.
As he talked, every farmer nodded. Slowly, steadily. Bhupen felt great. They all agreed!
At the end he said, "So you'll start next week?" More nodding.
Sumit, the senior officer who'd worked there for years, pulled him aside. "They're nodding because they're listening. It's polite. Not a yes."
Bhupen was confused. "But they nodded at everything."
"Exactly. Now ask them with words."
Bhupen went back. "Ramlal-ji, what worries you about the pipes?"
Ramlal took a breath. "The cost. And my son says the rats will eat them."
Two others agreed. Then the real questions came.
Bhupen wrote "nod = listening, not yes" at the top of his notebook.

qa.q: What did Ramlal say his son thought about the pipes?
qa.a: His son says the rats will eat them.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling while the farmers nodded?
qa.a: Bhupen felt pleased and confident, believing the nods meant everyone agreed.

qa.q: What did Sumit advise, and why did it help?
qa.a: He advised asking with words, because the nods showed polite attention, not agreement, and asking brought out the farmers' real worries.

qa.q: How did the farmers mean their nods?
qa.a: They meant "we're listening," as a polite sign of attention, not a promise to start.

grounding: The scene shows nodding meaning attention rather than agreement, and a young adult learning to clarify with words.

passage:
In their first week as exchange students in Sofia, Siddiq and Mei went to a kiosk to ask about the bus. Mei pointed at the map. "Does the number 94 go to the university?"
The woman at the kiosk shook her head from side to side.
Mei sighed. "No. Okay, let's find another bus."
Siddiq stopped her. "Wait. Our orientation leader said in Bulgaria a shake can mean yes and a nod can mean no. Let's check."
Mei looked doubtful. "Really?"
Siddiq turned back and said, slowly, "94. University. Yes? Da?"
The woman smiled. "Da, da. Yes. 94." And she shook her head again.
Mei laughed in disbelief. "So the shake was a yes!"
"Apparently. Though our leader also said some people here use the other way now, with foreigners. So..."
"So we always ask with words."
They caught the 94. It went straight to the university.

qa.q: Which bus number went to the university?
qa.a: The 94.

qa.q: What was Mei feeling when the woman shook her head?
qa.a: Mei felt disappointed and a little frustrated, thinking the answer was no.

qa.q: What did Siddiq do that avoided a mistake?
qa.a: He remembered that nods and shakes can be reversed there and clarified with words, asking "Yes? Da?"

qa.q: How did the kiosk woman mean her head shake?
qa.a: She meant yes, as the head shake can in Bulgaria, even though Mei read it as no.

grounding: The scene shows a head shake meaning yes in Bulgaria, and young adults clarifying with words in a cross-cultural exchange.

passage:
Bhupen volunteered at the international students' office at his university in Delhi. On Monday, a new student from abroad, Kofi, came in to register for courses.
Bhupen explained the whole process: forms, deadlines, the fee counter. Kofi nodded steadily the whole time. "Great, all clear?" Bhupen asked. Kofi nodded again.
The next day, Kofi came back. He'd gone to the wrong building and missed the deadline for one form.
Anjali, the coordinator, sat down with both of them. "Kofi, when Bhupen explained, you were nodding. Did that mean you understood?"
Kofi smiled, a little embarrassed. "It meant I was listening. Where I grew up, you nod to show respect while someone speaks. I didn't want to interrupt."
Anjali turned to Bhupen. "So from now on, we ask them to tell us back the steps. In words."
Bhupen nodded. Then laughed. "And that nod means yes."

qa.q: What did Kofi miss?
qa.a: The deadline for one form.

qa.q: What was Kofi feeling when he came back the next day?
qa.a: Kofi felt a little embarrassed, since his respectful nods had been taken as full understanding.

qa.q: What new step did Anjali introduce?
qa.a: Asking students to repeat the steps back in words, instead of relying on nods.

qa.q: What would change if Bhupen had asked Kofi to repeat the steps on Monday?
qa.a: Bhupen would have learned that the nods meant respectful listening, not understanding, and Kofi would not have missed the form deadline.

grounding: The scene shows nodding meaning attention rather than agreement across cultures, and clarifying with words.

passage:
Dear Bidisha,
Week two of the internship in Sofia, and I have already made a fool of myself, gently, luckily.
On Monday I asked Petar, who runs the lab stores, whether I could borrow the spare microscope. He shook his head side to side, so I said, "Oh, okay, sorry," and walked off. A minute later he came after me, puzzled, carrying the microscope! Here that head movement can mean yes.
Then on Wednesday I presented my project plan and everyone nodded along, so I assumed they agreed. Afterwards my supervisor told me the nods only meant "we are following you", and she had real doubts about my sample size.
So now I ask in words: "Is that a yes?" People laugh, but it works.
I do miss our head wobble at home, which means about ten things at once!
Love,
Rashmi

qa.q: What did Rashmi want to borrow from Petar?
qa.a: The spare microscope.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel when Petar came after her carrying the microscope?
qa.a: Rashmi felt embarrassed but amused, seeing that the head shake had meant yes here, though at home it would have read as a refusal.

qa.q: What did Rashmi start doing to avoid these mix-ups?
qa.a: Asking in words, such as "Is that a yes?", instead of trusting a nod or a shake in a new place.

qa.q: How might the supervisor have seen the team's nods during Rashmi's presentation?
qa.a: To the supervisor the nods simply meant the team was listening, so her doubts about the sample size still stood and needed to be said later.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult learning that nods can show attention rather than agreement, that head movements can carry reversed meanings abroad, and that words settle it.
